Second Sunni cleric killed in Iran in less than a week. Sunni Baluch cleric Molavi Yousef Gorgij was killed by unknown assailants outside his home in Zahedan, Iranian state media reported on Monday, the second killing of a Sunni cleric in Iran in less than a week.

Resistance born from Mahsa Amini’s death endures, UN rapporteur says. UN Special Rapporteur on Iran Mai Sato said the movement born from Mahsa “Jina” Amini’s death in Iran’s morality police custody remains alive four years on, despite another deadly crackdown and continued enforcement of mandatory hijab rules.

US sanctions Russia’s VTB Bank over Iran ties as financial crackdown widens. The United States on Monday imposed new Iran-related sanctions on Russia’s VTB Bank on Monday, accusing the already heavily sanctioned lender of helping Tehran evade restrictions through banking relationships and payment arrangements.

US, Iran hint at talks even as sanctions tighten and Hormuz tensions stay high. The United States and Iran both signaled openness to renewed negotiations Monday, even as Washington intensified its financial pressure campaign and conflicting accounts of incidents around the Strait of Hormuz underscored the mistrust surrounding any diplomatic opening.

Iran's Saudi leverage could become its liability. Iran has gained leverage over Saudi Arabia as Houthi advances and attacks put pressure on the kingdom’s territory and oil routes. But Riyadh is responding more forcefully, raising the risk that Tehran’s advantage could provoke a military backlash that ultimately weakens it.

Xi’s BRICS peace call sparks debate in Iran over China’s role in war. China’s call for a collective BRICS role in restoring peace in the Persian Gulf and Middle East has triggered debate in Iran over whether Beijing is preparing to mediate between Tehran and Washington.

US seeks $61 million in cryptocurrency tied to Iran oil sales. US prosecutors are seeking the forfeiture of about $61 million in cryptocurrency that came from black-market sales of sanctioned Iranian crude oil and petroleum products and was intended to finance Iran's government and military, including the Revolutionary Guards.

Iranian security forces arrest three Baha’is in Shiraz, source says. Iranian security forces arrested three Baha’i citizens during raids on their homes in Shiraz, southwestern Iran, on Monday and transferred them to an undisclosed location, Iran International has learned.

Islamic Republic asks public to identify opponents abroad. The Islamic Republic has launched a platform asking citizens to identify and report opponents living abroad. Iranians met it with ridicule, pointing to how deeply the state's own security apparatus has been infiltrated.

Women face forced undressing, breast touching at Iran's Evin Prison. Female political prisoners at Iran's Evin Prison face increasingly invasive body searches involving forced undressing and breast touching, leading some to forgo medical treatment and visits, sources told Iran International.

EU Parliament names Iran among states behind hybrid attacks on Europe. The European Parliament on Tuesday named Iran among countries it said were involved in hybrid attacks targeting Europe, including cyberattacks, sabotage, espionage and signal jamming.

Hormuz traffic plunges ahead of Iran-China talks. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz fell sharply as Iran prepared diplomatic talks in China, while attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to Persian Gulf cloud infrastructure underscored the widening consequences of the war on Tuesday.

After Muscat collapse, Tehran argues over what comes next. Iranian newspapers that agree on almost nothing agreed on Monday that the Muscat talks had collapsed. Kayhan, Shargh and Donya-ye Eghtesad all reported it, and the argument has already moved to what Tehran does next.

January's unfinished love stories: Lives severed by Iran protest killings. Eight months after Iran's January protests, the partners left behind by some of those killed are recounting lives abruptly divided by gunfire – marriages measured in months or days, anniversaries spent at graves and final embraces they never knew were their last.

Tehran political circles see US hand in postponement of Oman Hormuz talks. Iranian lawmakers, hardline media and analysts have blamed Washington for postponing Oman-hosted talks on Strait of Hormuz shipping arrangements, despite officials attributing the delay to regional objections and Saudi concerns over Yemen.

Iranian court upholds death sentence for another protest detainee. An Iranian appeals court has upheld the death sentence of Ali Rahimi Rigi, a 32-year-old detainee from the January protests, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

‘This is the cost you must pay’: Iran accused of denying food to death-row twin. Twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi have been tortured in detention and threatened with sexual violence, while death-row Taraneh is now being denied food in retaliation for family advocacy, their cousin told Iran International.

A generation shaped by Woman, Life, Freedom refuses to go back. Four years after Mahsa “Jina” Amini’s death in Iran’s morality police custody sparked the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, teenagers who watched her name become a rallying cry have grown up amid repression but beyond many of the social and political boundaries of pre-2022 Iran.

Security forces deploy as shops in western Iran strike on Mahsa Amini anniversary. Iranian security forces fanned out across several western cities on Wednesday as shopkeepers shut down businesses to mark the fourth anniversary of the death of Mahsa Amini, according to videos and messages sent to Iran International.

Iran used state machinery to crush 2022 uprising, Amnesty says. Iranian state authorities organized a systematic, high-level campaign of murder, torture, and sexual violence to crush the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, according to a 1,000-page investigation published by Amnesty International on Wednesday.

Shot and left for dead, Iran protester faces 26th surgery. Twenty-five surgeries have failed to end the ordeal of a protester shot during January demonstrations in Iran, with a severe infection still spreading through the wounded leg and a 26th operation now planned, Iran International learned.

US officials met Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman - Reuters. US officials met representatives of Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman over the weekend, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing five sources familiar with the matter, days after the group seized a strategic stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast.

Iranian women recall the first time they went out uncovered. Four years after the Woman, Life, Freedom protests, Iran International asked women on Instagram to describe the first time they went out without a headscarf. The answers came back in the same four registers: fear, freedom, grief and solidarity.

Mahsa’s dandelion: step by step through Iran's Woman, Life, Freedom. Mahsa Amini’s death in September 2022 set off something that could not be put back in its box. Woman, Life, Freedom challengeed the foundations of the Islamic Republic. This interactive project retraces the uprising, what was lost, but also what survived and what changed.

From Halkbank to Golden Global: Iran sanctions and Turkey’s banking ties. Turkey has stepped in to take control of shareholder rights at a bank accused by Washington of helping Tehran turn oil revenues into cash and gold: the latest chapter in a decades-long story linking Turkish banking, US sanctions and Iranian money.
Mahsa Amini and the century-long struggle of Iranian women. In September 2022, the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in the custody of Iran’s morality police ignited a fire that still burns.

Calls to quit NPT grow in Iran as critics warn of strategic trap. Calls for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty are gaining ground among hardliners after the IAEA referred the country to the UN Security Council and its nuclear chief was barred from attending the agency’s annual conference in Vienna.

Guinée-France : pourquoi Paris continue de ménager le régime de Mamadi Doumbouya. Malgré les accusations de répression qui visent le pouvoir en place à Conakry, Paris assume le choix du dialogue. Une stratégie diplomatique qui s’explique aussi par le poids économique croissant de la Guinée, portée par le boom minier.

Fouzi Lekjaâ : « Premier ministre ? Je vais vous dire une chose, je n’y ai jamais réfléchi ». Depuis son ralliement au PAM, et à moins de deux semaines des législatives du 23 septembre, le très médiatique ministre délégué au Budget et patron de la fédération de football attire tous les regards. Pourquoi est-il entré dans l’arène politique ? Envisage-t-il la primature ? Quelles ambitions nourrit-il pour la Coupe du monde que le royaume accueillera en 2030 ? Qu’a-t-il à dire sur la très polémique finale de la CAN contre le Sénégal et ses relations avec Gianni Infantino ? Interview exclusive.

« Historique », « systémique », « populaire » : tout ce qu’il faut savoir sur l’entrée en Bourse de la raffinerie Dangote. Aliko Dangote introduit sa raffinerie en Bourse dès le 14 septembre, visant 1,62 milliard de dollars. Une opération qui pourrait devenir la plus grande IPO de l’histoire africaine.

Présidentielle au Nigeria : la détention d’El-Rufai prive l’opposition de toute velléité de victoire. Personnage haut en couleur de l’opposition nigériane, Nasir El-Rufai croupit en prison depuis février dernier. À moins d’un an des élections, des voix commencent à s’élever pour dénoncer une manœuvre politique du pouvoir.

Entre Glencore et Mercuria, jusqu’où ira la bataille pour les minerais critiques ?. Longtemps dominé par les négociants historiques comme Glencore, le marché des minerais africains voit émerger une nouvelle concurrence. Mercuria, venu de l’énergie, accélère dans le cuivre, le cobalt et le zinc. Une rivalité à l’œuvre en Guinée et en RDC.

Cameroun : Alamine Ousmane Mey, l’électron libre du pouvoir. Encarté au sein du RDPC, au pouvoir, le ministre de l’Économie Alamine Ousmane Mey joue sa propre partition, bien à distance des intrigues qui rythment le quotidien de Yaoundé. Proche de Franck Biya, cet énigmatique banquier, fils d’un ancien baron du Nord peut-il peser sur la succession de Paul Biya ?

Sénégal : face à Starlink, Sonatel pousse l’État à faire respecter les règles. Le 7 septembre, la Cour suprême du Sénégal a suspendu Starlink après un recours déposé par Sonatel. L’opérateur historique dénonce des irrégularités dans l’attribution de la licence de la filiale d’Elon Musk et appelle l’État mettre à jour la régulation de ce type d’acteur.

Niger : en écartant le général Barmou, Abdourahamane Tiani veut reprendre la main sur l’armée. Quelques semaines après la mutinerie d’une partie des forces spéciales, les 28 et 29 août, le chef de la junte nigérienne a procédé à un vaste remaniement de la hiérarchie militaire. Un premier signal de la réponse du pouvoir à la mutinerie qui a secoué Niamey.

Mali : Kamissa Camara, du cœur du pouvoir à l’analyse des coups d’État. Elle fut, à 35 ans, la plus jeune ministre des Affaires étrangères du Mali, juste avant le coup d’État de 2020 qui renversa le pouvoir d’Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. Désormais, Kamissa Camara cherche à comprendre les motivations des militaires qui ont pris le pouvoir à Bamako, mais aussi à Ouagadougou.

Cameroun : comment le complexe d’Olembe s’est transformé en gouffre financier. Le projet devait être le symbole du Cameroun qui réussit quand le pays a reçu la CAN, en 2022. Mais le chantier n’a jamais été terminé et les litiges s’accumulent entre les entreprises de construction successives et l’État. Une bombe à retardement politique.

Bolt, Yango, Gozem… Qui saura profiter du retrait progressif d’Uber en Afrique ?. Côte d’Ivoire, Tanzanie, Nigeria, Ouganda… Le géant américain des voitures de transport avec chauffeur (VTC) réduit progressivement sa présence sur le continent, ouvrant la voie à une multitude d’opérateurs aux stratégies d’acquisition aussi agressives que diverses.

Jared Kushner, le Maroc et les milliards promis des accords d’Abraham. De retour au premier plan des négociations sur Gaza, le gendre et envoyé spécial du président américain veut adosser la relance des accords d’Abraham à l’injection de capitaux privés. Six ans après la reconnaissance américaine de la marocanité du Sahara occidental, que peut encore y gagner Rabat ?

Afrique-ONU : 5 questions pour comprendre les enjeux de la 81e Assemblée générale. Succession d’António Guterres, guerres au Soudan et dans l’est de la RDC, épidémie d’Ebola… La grand-messe onusienne s’ouvre le 22 septembre à New York et, cette année encore, des dossiers africains majeurs sont à suivre.
Aérien : Congo Airways peut-elle sortir de la crise ?. La compagnie aérienne de RDC est au bord du gouffre. Si le gouvernement a lancé un plan de relance en mars, reste à savoir s’il sera suffisant.

Massad Boulos à Alger : le Sahara en ligne de front, les hydrocarbures en arrière-plan. Le conseiller de Trump pour l’Afrique était de retour à Alger le 13 septembre pour sa troisième visite en cinq mois. Objectif : convaincre l’Algérie d’accepter le nouveau cadre onusien sur le Sahara occidental, tout en ouvrant la porte aux majors pétrolières américaines.

Entrée en Bourse : face aux doutes des marchés, Aliko Dangote a-t-il été trop gourmand ?. La valorisation de la raffinerie Dangote divise les analystes. Mais son directeur général explique pourquoi comparer Lekki aux raffineries européennes ou asiatiques n’a aucun sens.

« Tshisekedi nous a tendu un guet-apens » : en RDC, la mobilisation de l’opposition dégénère. À Kinshasa, la marche de la coalition C64 contre le changement de Constitution a tourné en affrontements entre manifestants, leaders d’opposition et des jeunes désignés comme membres du parti au pouvoir. Blessé, Martin Fayulu a mis en cause le chef de l’État.

Éthiopie : vers une nouvelle guerre dans le Tigré ?. Début août, de violents affrontements ont secoué l’ouest du Tigré, ravivant le spectre d’une nouvelle guerre. L’accord de Pretoria de 2022, censé sceller la paix, fait plus que vaciller.

Au Cameroun, une série d’auditions pourrait relancer l’affaire Fouda-Mbapou. L’affaire qui implique Joseph Fouda, conseiller de Paul Biya, et l’homme d’affaires Hervé Parfait Mbapou, soupçonné d’escroquerie en bande organisée, pourrait rebondir à Yaoundé. Une série d’auditions a lieu en septembre.

Comment la chute de la Samir a redéfini la politique énergétique marocaine. Dix ans après la faillite de son unique raffinerie, le Maroc continue de payer les pots cassés d’une privatisation mal ficelée. Pour autant, le pays entend consolider son approvisionnement en renforçant ses capacités de stockage.

La méthode Paul Kammogne Fokam, le Camerounais qui a bâti le géant bancaire Afriland loin des projecteurs. Fondateur d’Afriland First Bank, Paul Kammogne Fokam a bâti un empire bancaire en pariant sur l’épargne populaire. Portrait d’un pionnier discret, entre ambitions panafricaines et zones d’ombre.

Guinée-Côte d’Ivoire : dans les coulisses des retrouvailles entre Doumbouya et Ouattara. Le président guinéen a séjourné à Abidjan du 11 au 14 septembre où il s’est entretenu avec son homologue ivoirien. Sécurité frontalière, monnaie commune, opposants en exil… Plusieurs dossiers sensibles ont été évoqués lors de leur tête-à-tête.

« Ils ont vu les enfants, ils ont quand même tiré » : au Mali, enquête sur la guerre des drones. Pendant plusieurs mois, Jeune Afrique et Bellingcat ont enquêté, avec la participation de The Sentry, sur les frappes de drones menées par l’armée malienne et les Russes d’Africa Corps. Au moins un quart d’entre elles font des victimes civiles. La face cachée d’une impitoyable reconquête.

De Washington à Abou Dhabi, dans les coulisses du roadshow financier de Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Accord avec le FMI en poche, le président sénégalais joue la carte de la diplomatie financière. Tambour battant, il cherche à convaincre créanciers et investisseurs de parier sur le redressement du Sénégal.

Maroc : ce qui retarde l’introduction en Bourse de Dislog, le groupe de Moncef Belkhayat. À quelques mois de l’échéance prévue, l’entrepreneur attend toujours le visa du régulateur pour l’introduction en Bourse de Dislog, navire amiral du géant H&S Group. Déterminé à réaliser l’IPO d’ici à décembre, l’ancien ministre s’attelle désormais à bétonner son dossier en répondant à des compléments d’information.

Guinée équatoriale : faux coup d’État, mais vraies arrestations chez les Obiang. Après avoir affirmé avoir localement déjoué un putsch, Malabo a ensuite démenti sa propre version. Mais les arrestations dans les familles de l’opposition en exil ont bien eu lieu et quatre personnes sont toujours détenues.

Au Cameroun, comment la guerre des clans autour de Paul Biya a fracturé les services de renseignements. Le monde du renseignement camerounais est devenu l’un des théâtres des rivalités entourant le président. Première victime : la Direction générale de la recherche extérieure (DGRE). Naguère redoutée, elle n’est plus que l’ombre d’elle-même.

Législatives au Maroc, le ton se durcit et certains partis jouent déjà l’après-scrutin. Alors que le RNI et le PAM règlent leurs comptes, l’Istiqlal consolide ses points d’ancrage et le PJD appelle au vote sanction. Le Mouvement populaire et l’USFP, quant à eux, cherchent l’espace qui leur permettra de peser. À quelques jours du vote, le ton de la campagne s’est nettement tendu.

États-Unis-Mali : des élus américains demandent un encadrement du rapprochement Trump-Goïta. Face à la propagation du Jnim au Sahel, des élus républicains et démocrates américains veulent encadrer le rapprochement entre l’administration Trump et le Mali. Un projet de loi bipartisan exige une stratégie diplomatique transparente pour contrer l’expansion jihadiste.

Pourquoi l’échec de Drapor pèse toujours sur la souveraineté économique du Maroc. Longtemps symbole de souveraineté industrielle du royaume, la société spécialisée dans le dragage incarne désormais un des échecs retentissants de la politique de privatisation des années 1990. Un dossier qui a encore des répercussions aujourd’hui.

Immigration : pourquoi les candidats à l’exil du continent africain se reportent sur la route des îles Canaries. A la fin d’août 2026, 1 046 personnes ont été secourues dans l’océan Atlantique en une semaine. Elles tentaient de rejoindre les îles Canaries à bord d’embarcations de fortune. « Le Monde » s’est rendu sur place, au printemps 2026, au plus près de candidats à l’exil.

La raffinerie nigériane d’Aliko Dangote au seuil de la plus grande entrée en Bourse d’Afrique. De Lagos à Nairobi en passant par Johannesburg, les milieux financiers africains s’enthousiasment pour l’introduction à la Bourse de Lagos de la raffinerie de Lekki, qui s’ouvrira lundi 14 septembre sur fond de bénéfices en forte hausse et d’une géopolitique mondiale favorable.

En Ethiopie, le changement climatique pousse les éleveurs pastoraux à se convertir à l’agriculture vivrière : « C’est loin d’être une solution miracle ». Dans le sud-est du pays, les épisodes de sécheresse, toujours plus intenses, menacent l’existence des pasteurs nomades. Certains ont choisi de se sédentariser pour cultiver la terre.

« Les accords d’Abraham ont plutôt encouragé la guerre que la paix au Moyen-Orient ». Six ans après leur signature, les accords d’Abraham, loin de généraliser la normalisation israélo-arabe, ont aggravé les dissensions au Moyen-Orient, analyse l’historien Jean-Pierre Filiu dans sa chronique au « Monde ».

A Dakar, l’art de la sape vise le « 100 % made in Sénégal ». L’élégance est partout dans les rues de la capitale sénégalaise. Elle encourage la création, qui reste dépendante des importations de fibres textiles.

En Méditerranée centrale, une chasse à l’homme en haute mer sponsorisée par l’UE. « Le Monde » a embarqué en juillet à bord de l’« Ocean-Viking », le navire de sauvetage affrété par SOS Méditerranée. L’ONG française dénonce l’intensification de la violence en mer contre les migrants et les humanitaires de la part d’acteurs libyens soutenus et financés par l’Union européenne.

« C’est une manière de nous chasser sans le dire » : à l’université, les étudiants non européens confrontés à la flambée de leurs droits d’inscription. Instaurés en 2019, les frais différenciés d’inscription aux universités publiques françaises pour les étudiants extracommunautaires ne sont appliqués réellement que depuis la rentrée 2026. Des droits 16 fois plus cher, qui pénalisent en majorité les étudiants africains.

Au Mali, au moins 50 militaires et cinq mercenaires russes tués jeudi dans une attaque djihadiste. Depuis 2012, le Mali fait face à une profonde crise sécuritaire, nourrie notamment par les violences de groupes djihadistes, de leurs alliés indépendantistes touareg du Front de libération de l’Azawad et de groupes criminels communautaires.

« Il n’avait aucun problème de santé » : dans les prisons tunisiennes, de nombreuses morts suspectes après un été caniculaire. Les mois de juillet et d’août ont été marqués dans toute la Tunisie par de fortes chaleurs, des coupures d’eau et d’électricité, et des pénuries d’eau minérale. Une situation particulièrement éprouvante dans les prisons, sans qu’aucun bilan officiel du nombre de décès ait été communiqué

« Plutôt mourir que d’être renvoyé en Libye » : l’odyssée infernale des migrants en Méditerranée centrale. « Le Monde » a embarqué en juillet à bord de l’« Ocean Viking », le navire de sauvetage affrété par SOS Méditerranée. Secourus en haute mer par l’ONG française, des rescapés témoignent d’un cycle de violences sans fin depuis leurs pays d’origine jusqu’à la Méditerranée.

Un homme d’affaires malien, Oumar Gambi, victime d’un spectaculaire cambriolage à 1 million d’euros dans un palace parisien. Des voleurs se sont introduits, en escaladant la façade du Plaza Athénée, dans la chambre de l’entrepreneur malien, célèbre dans son pays, et qui gravite dans l’entourage du président congolais, Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Les Mondiaux d’athlétisme 2029 organisés à Nairobi, une première pour le continent africain. La capitale du Kenya a été désignée, mardi, ville hôte de la compétition reine. Dans un communiqué, la fédération internationale rappelle entre autres que le pays est l’une des « grandes nations de ce sport ».

Ebola en RDC : l’épidémie continue de s’étendre de façon « exponentielle » dans le nord-est du pays ; la situation épidémiologique reste « hétérogène », alerte l’OMS. Le nombre de morts hebdomadaires a presque doublé dans le Nord-Kivu, alors que la transmission a ralenti dans d’autres régions. L’institution recense 3 475 morts sur 7 200 cas confirmés.

Du Mali à la Gambie, les partisans de l’excision en campagne : « Une fille excisée aura moins de pulsions sexuelles et sera une épouse fidèle ». Une campagne numérique appelant à « protéger » l’excision au Mali est devenue virale à la mi-août. La preuve pour de nombreux observateurs que le combat mené sur le continent pour faire interdire les mutilations génitales féminines, qui tuent chaque année des dizaines de milliers de filles et de femmes, est loin d’être gagné.

Yasser Mounbir, figure de la scène graffiti au Maroc, risque la prison ferme pour avoir dessiné le roi Mohammed VI. Incarcéré depuis trois mois, l’artiste de 22 ans doit comparaître mercredi 16 septembre devant le tribunal correctionnel de Casablanca. Ses soutiens dénoncent un tour de vis des autorités, alors que les poursuites pour « outrage » se multiplient.

Ornella Moderan, chercheuse : « Exciser, c’est perpétuer une certaine idée de la virilité au détriment de l’intégrité physique des femmes ». Alors qu’une campagne numérique prônant l’excision est devenue virale en août sur les réseaux sociaux maliens, la politologue Ornella Moderan analyse, dans un entretien au « Monde », les enjeux qui entourent les mutilations génitales féminines.

Ebola en RDC : des « signes encourageants » dans la lutte contre l’épidémie, qui « continue de progresser et de tuer », déclare l’OMS. Le directeur général de l’organisation, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, a annoncé mercredi que les essais cliniques sur les traitements et les vaccins contre la maladie à virus s’accéléraient, alors que la RDC connaît la pire flambée de son histoire.

Soudan : au moins 82 morts dans l’effondrement d’une mine d’or. La mine d’Al-Zaraa s’est effondrée mardi, et « un nombre indéterminé » de personnes restent coincées sous les décombres, a déclaré, mercredi, une source des Forces de soutien rapide à l’Agence France-Presse.

En Algérie, l’enseignement du français en primaire relégué au second plan au profit de l’anglais. La réforme portée par le ministre de l’éducation a suscité une levée de boucliers dans les milieux francophones. Mais elle est soutenue par les partisans d’une mise à jour du système éducatif algérien.

Israël et le Maroc vont ouvrir des ambassades dans leurs pays respectifs, annonce la diplomatie de l’Etat hébreu. Le ministère israélien a aussi annoncé que des accords économiques seraient conclus entre les deux pays, qui disposent de bureaux de liaison, avant la fin de 2026, ainsi qu’une extension des vols directs entre le Maroc et Israël.

DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no regional aspirations', intended for collective deterrence. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that the Makkah Defence Alliance — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence. The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English ’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson. During the show, aired during the early hours of Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about Pakistan’s commitments under the agreement. “It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said. Watson then asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied. “It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”. Elaborating further, he said the countries part of the alliance had independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances. “So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he added. At that, Watson asked, “But does it contain any mutual defence obligation?” In his short reply to the question, Lt Gen Chaudhry remarked, “The text that has been made public by the leadership of the three countries enunciates that very clearly and it’s interpretation is quite clear.” Asked how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalisation of defensive commitments was never made public in any discourse. “You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details […] What you’re asking is the how part — that how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression. “That is always part of the operational classification and security […] What you’re asking is that how it will be done. It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualise it,” he said. Specifically asked whether the military spokesperson saw the alliance “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s relationship with China, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that it complemented Islamabad-Beijing ties. “We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Turkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it. That’s how historic these relationships are. We have formalised that. “Nobody has any problem with that. Everyone understands that this is defensive. Everyone understands it is for maintaining stability and peace in the region. And all the three countries that are part of it, they have a wonderful relationship with China,” he said. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture. He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability. “It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. “This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence. “But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated. The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years. Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo. From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point. The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained. US-Iran mediation and Pakistan’s ‘unique position’ During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between the United States and Iran and whether the Makkah Defence Alliance complicated Islamabad’s position towards Tehran. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied such was not the case, adding that the alliance was based on decades-old strategic ties. “This alliance is a formalisation of that strategic relationship in a peculiar environment,” he said, reiterating that the pact was based on collective deterrence. The defence pact, he said, had no offensive or aggressive element and was purely defensive in nature. Asked why Pakistan had opted to play the role of a mediator in the ongoing Middle East conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, he succinctly stated, “For regional peace.” Lt Gen Chaudhry then added that stability stemmed from peace and Pakistan was a proponent of peace in the region. Moreover, he continued, Pakistan had a “unique position” in this case because of its policy of alignment and engagement with countries across the world. Hence, it could play the role of an “objective arbiter of peace and an honest broker of peace”. To a question about progress on the mediation front and towards a settlement, Lt Gen Chaudhry explained that one of the prerequisites of good mediation was remaining objective and neutral. “So it’s not for us as a mediator to start commenting on things that are happening or that are bound to happen,” he said, adding that Pakistan’s political and military leadership had been reaching out to all the parties so that “better sense prevails and, instead of a military solution, we come to a negotiated outcome of this very complex situation”. Watson then pointed to the possibility of the US and Iran rejecting Pakistan’s proposal and asked whether Islamabad was prepared to continue its mediation in that case. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied, “Is there any other way of resolving this conflict other than [through] mediation? Is there any other desirable way of doing that?” He stressed the need for a “negotiated, peaceful outcome”, adding that those who could mediate objectively and sincerely between the two sides must continue their efforts. Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the conflict spilling over towards its western frontiers, Lt Gen Chaudhry answered that as far as Pakistan’s borders, territorial integrity and sovereignty were concerned, “we are very confident and very self-reliant on our security”. There were always concerns of any conflict spiralling horizontally or vertically, he said, adding that not just Pakistan, but the entire world at large was feeling the impact of the conflict. “So, there are [always] concerns in multiple domains”, but Pakistan was “fully confident of taking care of whatever nefarious designs come out of that towards” it, he said. Asked whether Pakistan aimed to become a regional mediator or was simply trying to prevent a regional war from reaching its own doorstep, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Pakistan is interested in regional peace and stability, because peace and stability are essential for development, for human development, for prosperity and for the citizens of Pakistan and the region.” And if the “mediation is for peace, […] and we’ll always be there”. Prospects of dialogue with India Watson then came to the brief military conflict between Pakistan and India in May last year, and asked what lessons Pakistan’s military had learned from the episode. Lt Gen Chaudhry replied that what was more important were the lessons Pakistan and its military taught during that conflict. He said that a military conflict between two nuclear countries, especially neighbours, was “out of question”. “It’s a sheer, I would say, a sort of mad idea,” he said, adding that Pakistan also showed that India made a “strategic folly” in May last year. Asked whether he believed India had learned that lesson, Lt Gen Chaudhry replied it was for the Indian side to answer. “Our job in Pakistan is to keep on reminding them of that lesson,” he said, adding that the other side had a “hubristic mindset” and the Indian military was “deeply politicised”. In India, he continued, there was a propensity of externalising their internal problems, giving the example of minorities facing oppression. On the other hand, he said, there was the Kashmir issue, which was an “external problem” that New Delhi wanted to “internalise through repression”. The military’s spokesperson added that Pakistan continued to give out the message to India that it believed in “peace on equal terms” and that it was a rational and objective player. Pakistan believes in regional peace, but if India has any “misconceptions about [imposing] regional hegemony through military aggression, results of that would be beyond their imagination”, he warned. Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan had showed India and the world in May last year that it had the capability and resolve to dominate and control an escalation. “And we’ll do it again,” he added. Asked whether there were any realistic prospects of restoring sustained military-to-military communication with India, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Yes, of course.” He added that communication between the directors general of military operations had remained effective during the May conflict and beyond. “Communication is always good. We must communicate, we must engage, but that engagement has to be done on equal terms while respecting each other’s integrity and sovereignty,” he said. To a question about resuming dialogue with India, he said it was for the political leadership to decide. But dialogue, he said, had to be on equal terms. “Dialogue cannot be, or engagement cannot be to provide a cover for the ongoing state-sponsored Indian terrorism in Pakistan, for the ongoing aggression,” he emphasised. ‘Only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world’ Coming to Afghanistan, Watson asked about the Pakistani military’s preferred end state with the Afghan Taliban. “I think the military’s end state is actually part of Pakistan’s end state that the political leadership sets. So, there is no separate military end state. “So, there are Pakistan’s objectives and desire, which are primarily the domain of the Pakistan’s political leadership and an expression of the will of the people of Pakistan. And what that is that we want — no interference, no terrorism from Afghanistan in Pakistan. So that’s the foundation,” he said. Asked what options Pakistan considered legitimate for preventing cross-border attacks in case of the failure of diplomacy, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Right of self-defence is enshrined in the Article 51 of the United Nations; right of self-defence is given to each nation state of the world.” He added that the Pakistani state had an obligation to defend the lives, honour and property of its citizens. To that end, “all that is necessary will be done and is being done”. In this connection, he detailed Pakistan’s counter-terrorism measures and said the country’s counter-terrorism campaign was the “only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world”. “Because we are the bulwark state against” terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, he said. Lt Gen Chaudhry also mentioned that in the current year, 42,000 intelligence-based operations (IBOs) had been carried out and 2,100 terrorists had been killed. Towards the programme’s end, Watson steered the discussion towards Balochistan, on which Lt Gen Chaudhry said there was no insurgency in the province. “There’s just terrorism,” he said, adding that the military had clarity on that, tactically and strategically. He said of the 42,000 IBOs, over 32,000 were conducted in Balochistan and security forces remained engaged in “taking out the so-called proxies who associate themselves with Balochistan and have got nothing to do with it”. Regarding strategic clarity, he said the government, people of Balochistan and the military understood that the way to deal with terrorism was to kill terrorists and “embrace the people of Balochistan”.

JI chief warns talks with govt may end after 4th round if decision on abolishing petroleum levy delayed. KARACHI: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Wednesday warned that ongoing talks with the government over the petroleum levy may end if the levy is not withdrawn soon. The talks between the government and JI began on September 7 after the two sides agreed to form committees, comprising experts and leaders, to discuss recommendations for reducing the petroleum levy and providing relief to the public. So far, three rounds of talks have been held, with the fourth round scheduled for 6pm today (Wednesday) in Islamabad. According to a statement issued by the party, the JI chief spoke in Karachi earlier in the day, where he rejected the government’s fuel relief scheme and demanded that the levy be abolished, “rather than replaced with temporary relief schemes”. “If the government continues delaying and does not abolish the petroleum levy, today’s talks will be the last round,” Rehman was quoted as saying, reiterating that the party will go ahead with its march to Islamabad on Sept 20. As per the statement, Rehman said the government collected Rs1,567 billion through the petroleum levy annually but announced only Rs25bn in relief for the public. He described the package as inadequate and questioned its proposed implementation through weekly fuel distribution, the statement added. Rehman slammed “lockdown measures”. He added that the traders were “being pressured in the name of maintaining the system”. As per the statement, Rehman “called for an end to the practice of revising petroleum prices daily”. He voiced concern at the “frequent revisions”, which he said created difficulties for consumers and businesses. Speaking to the media, Rehman also outlined plans to hold “public meetings”, adding that a “large gathering” would be held in Karachi on Wednesday night, followed by rallies in Lahore on Thursday, and in Mardan and Peshawar on Friday. “The Islamabad march will not stop,” he was quoted as saying. Rehman urged the government not to disrupt peaceful and democratic struggle, according to the statement. Meanwhile, in a post on X, the party said that Wednesday’s round will be held in the Federal Secretariat at 6pm, with the JI delegation led by Liaquat Baloch and the government by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal. The government’s team will also include Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani. JI has been staging regular sit-ins in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and dozens of other locations across the country since August 16 to protest the levy and IPP agreements. The government levies Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Last week, the JI chief had warned the government that the ongoing protest would march towards Islamabad on September 20 if the levy was not withdrawn.

Police refute KP CM's claim of 'murder' conspiracy in Wazirabad, say constable was on security duty. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday claimed that his security detail had apprehended a man allegedly sent to kill him. Gujranwala Police, however, refuted the claim, saying the detained man was a constable deployed for the chief minister’s security. The KP chief minister has been visiting Punjab since Monday to mobilise party supporters ahead of the PTI’s nationwide protest scheduled for Sept 27. Earlier on Wednesday, Afridi issued a video statement , which he said was recorded shortly before 5am, giving his version of events. The KP CM alleged that hurdles were created during his stay in Sialkot, with power supplies cut off and the electricity generators at two residences he visited “ ruined ”. He subsequently travelled to Wazirabad. “They had sent an assassin after us with the intention to kill. He was in civil clothes. When we arrived in Wazirabad, my security team apprehended this armed individual, recovered a pistol from him, and handed him over to the local SHO (station house officer),” he claimed. Afridi reiterated his stance in an X post at 5:49am, saying his security team handed the “bearded man” over to SHO Saqlain after apprehending him. The KP CM recalled that he was supposed to spend the night in Sialkot, but the electricity was “cut off”. He added that power at two other locations was also disconnected, after which he travelled to Wazirabad. “Now, the electricity here has also been cut off. I cannot go anywhere else from here now,” the chief minister lamented. However, in separate statements, Gujranwala Police and Wazirabad City police station said the man was Constable Muqadas Ali, who had been deployed on security duty for Afridi. Gujranwala Police said the constable was “subjected to severe physical assault by members of the chief minister’s protection team”. “Importantly, Constable Muqadas Ali was allegedly assaulted in the presence of the SHO City Wazirabad, who intervened and after considerable effort, managed to rescue the constable. The SHO’s presence can also be clearly seen in footage and images from the scene,” the statement said. The police said the “misrepresentation of facts” and the constable’s “portrayal as a killer is a matter of serious concern”. According to Gujranwala Police, following the incident, “claims portraying Constable Ali as a ‘killer’ emerged from representatives” of the KP CM. “These claims misrepresent the facts, despite his identity having already been established at the scene and his departmental identity card having been presented.” The police asserted that “any baseless and factually incorrect portrayal of its personnel is unacceptable”. “Misrepresenting facts and portraying a police officer deployed on official duty as a killer is strongly condemnable,” it added. “It is a matter of serious concern that, after the incident, the constable was allegedly portrayed as a ‘murderer’, despite his identity and official duty being established at the spot,” the statement from Wazirabad City police said. Punjab Inf­ormation Minister Azma Bokhari also reiterated the police’s stance. “God knows why such fits of madness strike them as soon as they reach Wazirabad,” she quipped. On Nov 3, 2022, during PTI’s long march in Wazirabad, former premier Imran Khan and several others were injured in a gun attack , while one worker had lost his life. In 2025, a man was handed life imprisonment for the attack, while two others were acquitted. Punjab visit Wednesday was not the first episode of claims and counterclaims during the KP CM’s Punjab visit. On Monday night, Afridi alleged he was “ abducted ” by authorities in Lahore and later “thrown” by the roadside — a claim the Punjab government swiftly denied. In a video shared by Bokhari, Afridi could be seen voluntarily walking towards and boarding the police vehicle. He then refuses to dismount, while an individual can be heard asking the chief minister to “please leave the vehicle”. Afridi turned his Lahore visit into a full-fledged political showdown, lashing out at the Punjab government, refusing security and vowing to rid the country of “fake rulers” through a nationwide street movement on September 27. Speaking on Tuesday, CM Afridi alleged that Punjab police had blocked routes, arrested party workers and removed tents from a protest camp. On its part, the Punjab government has imposed a ban on gatherings across the province from September 13 to 17. District authorities had also issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. Additional input from Asif Chaudhry

OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Face for weaknesses 2 months before major hack. Rogue AI agents from OpenAI hijacked Hugging Face user accounts and probed the site itself for vulnerabilities as early as May, nearly two months before the July breach of the open-source repository drew global attention, according to researchers who reviewed the activity. The newly uncovered malicious activity showed that the rogue agents’ efforts to find a way into Hugging Face began earlier than publicly known. OpenAI had previously disclosed one aspect of the malicious activity — the theft of a Hugging Face user’s digital credential to access a biology-related file — in its public incident report last month, but researchers told Reuters the probing activity against Hugging Face appeared to go beyond what was described in the report. The activity was discovered by independent researcher Jonas Wiedermann-Moeller last week, he told Reuters . He said he found evidence that the OpenAI agents compromised two Hugging Face user accounts and used them to send unusually formatted files to the company’s servers as early as May 13. He and other researchers who reviewed the evidence said the behaviour resembled an attempt to map or test parts of Hugging Face’s network for ways to infiltrate, although they stressed there was no evidence the effort resulted in an actual breach. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had disclosed the May 13 event, privately notified Hugging Face about the activity flagged by Wiedermann-Moeller and was “committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as our review continues.” Hugging Face, recently acquired by chipmaker Nvidia, did not respond to requests for comment. Wiedermann-Moeller, a 27-year-old who lives in Bielefeld, Germany, said OpenAI’s failure to detect the May 13 probing at the time was a missed opportunity to prevent the subsequent hacking campaign, which has triggered a global reckoning over the power of artificial intelligence. “Imagine if they caught this behaviour in May,” he said in an interview. “It could’ve prevented the later incident, which was way bigger.” OpenAI has previously said that, with the benefit of hindsight, “some early signals” from its AI agents should have triggered an earlier response. ‘Clear warning sign’ Two outside experts who reviewed Wiedermann-Moeller’s findings said they were consistent with activity previously linked to OpenAI’s agents. SentinelOne senior threat researcher Tom Hegel said the account hijacking and subsequent probing matched known behaviour by the agents “to a tee.” Sydney Von Arx of the Nightingale Collective, an AI safety group, agreed with the attribution. Von Arx said the hacking amounted to a “clear warning sign” that could have helped prevent the breach in July. OpenAI has faced increasing scrutiny since the company disclosed on July 21 that rogue AI agents bypassed internal controls, reached the open internet and coordinated actions that OpenAI described as “an unprecedented cyber incident.” Since then, outside researchers have identified additional incidents alleged to involve OpenAI-linked agents, including activity affecting a dormant German wiki site and the RubyGems software package repository. OpenAI has acknowledged some of those incidents only after they were publicly reported by third parties. Two people familiar with the matter said that, in the case of RubyGems, OpenAI employees only realised its AI was responsible for the malicious activity after the Nightingale Collective found it. The additional discoveries have fueled questions among lawmakers and AI safety advocates about whether the full scope of the incidents has been identified. Some of America’s top AI executives have since called for a slowdown of AI development, citing, among other things, the threat of devastating cyberattacks by out-of-control agents. Wiedermann-Moeller said the latest findings reinforced calls for a temporary slowdown in the development of advanced AI systems. “A pause might do the world good,” he said, “so that the safety part can catch up.”

CDF Munir, US-based POWERUS discuss defence technology, cooperation. Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir on Wednesday discussed evolving trends in defence technology and potential areas of cooperation with United States-based defence and critical infrastructure company POWERUS, the military’s media wing said. The meeting focused on opportunities for collaboration in defence procurement, production and capacity building, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR). The POWERUS delegation was led by Robert Bret Velicovich. During the meeting, CDF Munir also highlighted the “importance of technological innovation and advanced solutions in strengthening national security and resilience.” The company, according to its website , “builds hardware and unified systems architecture that keep critical assets running in high-consequence environments.” Both sides expressed interest in further developing engagement in areas of mutual interest, added ISPR. In January, US and Pakistan army soldiers completed training at the National Counter-Terrorism Center during Exercise Inspired Gambit, which focused on combined infantry skills and tactics, and counterterrorism operations. In December last year, the US approved the sale of advanced technology and upgrade packages for Pakistan’s F-16 fighter aircraft, a deal valued at approximately $686 million.

South Africa pushes back on US visa curbs. South Africa on Wednesday hit back at new US visa restrictions over its racial equity policies, accusing the Trump administration of distorting its laws and further straining ties between Washington and one of Africa’s most influential powers. The dispute is the latest front in a broader clash over race, trade and diplomacy that has seen Washington cut aid, impose tariffs, expel South Africa’s ambassador and boycott a G20 summit in Johannesburg, all against the unresolved legacy of white minority rule. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the new visa restrictions would target those who promote “race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said Pretoria viewed the move “with concern” and that Washington was echoing narratives promoted by fringe groups opposed to South Africa’s post-apartheid reforms. “We reiterate that healing the divisions of the past and establishing a society based on democratic values, social justice and fundamental human rights is a constitutional imperative,” Lamola said in a statement. The US did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions but warned of further “severe” action. “This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter,” US ambassador to South Africa, Brent Bozell, said. ‘Hypocrisy’ President Donald Trump has criticised South Africa’s land reform and employment equity laws, which were introduced after the end of apartheid to address racial disparities that remain among the world’s widest. Trump has portrayed the measures as discriminatory against Afrikaners, the white minority descended largely from Dutch settlers, a claim Pretoria rejects. In 2025, he berated President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a “ white genocide ” in South Africa. While the US president has broadly cracked down on immigration, his administration has offered refugee status to thousands of white South Africans it says face persecution. Lamola rejected suggestions that the government was targeting any racial group, saying crime remained a national challenge affecting all South Africans. The opposition uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party, led by former president Jacob Zuma, also condemned the visa restrictions, calling them an affront to South Africa’s sovereignty. “The hypocrisy of Washington’s position is breathtaking. It lectures South Africa, while arming Israel amid the reported killing of more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza,” it said in a statement. Despite the tensions, Pretoria and Washington have remained engaged in efforts to thaw relations. “The discussions have highlighted the need for any resolution to consider South Africa’s unique circumstances and to respect its democracy, constitution, sovereignty, and the will of its people,” Lamola said. South Africa is the largest trading partner of the US on the African continent, with more than 500 US businesses and 30,000 US citizens based in the country. South Africa said last month it would offer a “generous” new trade deal to the United States as it seeks to avoid hefty tariffs that threaten job losses on top of a dire unemployment crisis.

PHF requests AHF to shift Asian Champions Trophy out of India or relocate Pakistan matches. The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) has formally asked the Asian Hockey Federation (AHF) to move next month’s men’s Asian Champions Trophy out of India or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue, citing the “sensitive bilateral situation” between the two countries. The request effectively rules out Pakistan playing their matches at the tournament’s scheduled venues in Jalandhar and Mohali unless the AHF agrees to the proposed change. PHF president Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani, who is also federal secretary of the Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination, confirmed to Dawn on Wednesday that the federation had formally approached the AHF. The development came two days after Wani had told Dawn that Pakistan’s proposed tour to India was subject to government clearance and that the PHF would abide by whatever decision the government took. Sources in the PHF said the latest decision to seek a neutral venue had been taken on the direction of the federal government. In an official statement issued on Wednesday, Wani said the request had been made to ensure a “safe, dignified and conducive environment” for Pakistan’s players and officials. “The Pakistan Hockey Federation has formally requested the Asian Hockey Federation to relocate the Men’s Asian Champions Trophy 2026 tournament or shift all of Pakistan’s matches to a neutral venue,” Wani said in the statement. The PHF chief, however, made it clear that Pakistan remained committed to the tournament and was willing to face India. “Pakistan remains fully committed to participating in the Asian Champions Trophy and international hockey and is ready to play against all FIH member nations, including India,” he said. The PHF president also said the federation hoped the AHF would consider the proposal positively to ensure Pakistan’s full participation in the tournament. The request comes two days after Indian Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said Pakistan would participate in the tournament, prompting the PHF to clarify that no decision had been taken on the team’s visit to India. Mann, according to a Press Trust of India (PTI) report, had said Pakistan would be among the six teams competing in the Asian Champions Trophy, scheduled to be held from Oct 27 to Nov 5. “There is no problem in multi-national tournaments. Maybe individual series [between India and Pakistan] cannot take place,” Mann said at an event in Mohali when asked about Pakistan’s participation and whether the requisite clearances had been obtained. The tournament is scheduled to feature hosts India, Pakistan, China, Japan, Malaysia and South Korea. Jalandhar is to host the opening ceremony and all league-stage matches from Oct 27 to Nov 2, while the semi-finals and final are scheduled to be played in Mohali on Nov 4 and 5. Pakistan’s proposed match against India is scheduled for Nov 1 in Jalandhar. The PHF’s latest move means that, while Pakistan is seeking to avoid playing its fixtures in India, it is not seeking to withdraw from the competition. The federation has specifically stated that it is prepared to play India and other FIH member nations at a neutral venue. Pakistan had also withdrawn from last year’s Junior World Cup in Tamil Nadu amid heightened tensions between the two countries.

‘New pathway for the future’: Quantum Valley Pakistan launched in Islamabad. Quantum Valley Pakistan, a project likened to America’s Silicon Valley, was launched in Islamabad on Wednesday, with Federal Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives Ahsan Iqbal as the chief guest. The Planning Ministry described Quantum Valley Pakistan as a project aimed at connecting academia, entrepreneurs, government and investors to turn “knowledge into solutions, startups into scalable ventures and innovation into national impact”. The project aims to create new pathways for Pakistani talent in AI, quantum computing, fintech, agritech, biotechnology, medtech, digital solutions and autonomous technologies, the ministry said. California’s venture capital firm Plug and Play and the Cambridge Innovation Centre collaborated with the government for the project. Addressing the launch ceremony, Iqbal said, “We are actually setting a new pathway for Pakistan’s future”. “Pakistan is ready for innovation takeoff,” he said. He stressed that this was not an ordinary collaboration, adding that the two companies would bring to Pakistan the “best of innovation in the world and the United States”. Describing the collaboration as a “unique opportunity” for Pakistan, Iqbal expressed hope for the growth of the country’s technology sector. He said that the paradigm of national progress had shifted in the 21st century, with “brain power” now being a key requirement for development. The planning minister added that the foundations for growth being established through Quantum Valley would allow Pakistan’s youth to compete with the youth of the world in terms of tech growth and startups. “Today, we stand at an inflection point,” Iqbal said, adding that in the past two years, Pakistan had seen many successes, namely Marka-i-Haq and recent diplomacy efforts in the US-Iran war . “In my lifetime, I had never seen that for an entire week, media from the US to Australia was only mentioning Islamabad,” he said, referring to the Islamabad talks in April. Successes achieved in defence and diplomacy, if not supplemented by a strong economy, can blur over time, Iqbal said. Alluding to Marka-i-Haq , Iqbal said the nation had to rise to the occasion of “ Marka-i-Taraqi ” and aim to build a $1 trillion economy by 2035 under the Uraan Pakistan programme. He further said the economy should grow to $3 trillion by 2047, when the country marks its centenary. Uraan Pakistan is an initiative of the Planning Ministry designed to advance key projects and reforms set out in the 5Es National Economic Transformation Plan. “These goals are ambitious but not impossible,” Iqbal said. Iqbal urged the nation to move away from the status quo and instead opt for a “transformational path”. The ceremony also included the inauguration of the Global Venture Acceleration Programme for local startups, under which they would receive mentorship over 15 weeks, along with a two-week global immersion in Silicon Valley or Boston.

Govt working to introduce virtual grid system, says power minister. ISLAMABAD: Power Minister Awais Leghari on Wednesday said the government was working to introduce a virtual grid system in the country, under which consumers would be able to generate and store electricity. Talking to the media after a National Assembly panel meeting, the minister said work on regulations for virtual grids had already started and that the regulations would be finalised by the last quarter of the current fiscal year. The minister said power distribution companies (Discos) had also been directed to install batteries on their grids as part of efforts to improve the power system and promote energy storage. “A battery revolution is coming to Pakistan as the government seeks to promote battery use and introduce a virtual grid system,” he said. “The government’s objective is to increase the use of batteries in the country’s power sector.” Earlier, the minister faced a tough time at the NA Standing Committee on Power meeting as committee chairman Muhammad Idrees questioned him about prolonged electricity load-shedding in the country. During the meeting, Leghari acknowledged that load-shedding was being carried out on around 3,500 of the country’s 14,500 feeders due to electricity theft and line losses. “Within a year, the government will shift load-shedding from feeders to transformers so that an entire feeder will not have to be shut down,” he said, adding that the government was also introducing an on-off control system for around 190,000 transformers. With the new system, he said, it would not be necessary to shut down an entire feeder, while consumers who regularly paid their electricity bills would not be affected. He said there was currently no additional load-shedding in the country. “The outages are mainly occurring due to faults caused by overloading of the power system.” Leghari said heavy investment was required to upgrade the power system and that approval from the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) would be sought for the upgrades. Regarding the energy situation, the minister said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had affected the Petroleum Division’s ability to receive LNG cargoes. He said the government was using locally produced gas for power generation. Explaining the decision to carry out load-shedding at night, Leghari asked, “Who will bear an additional electricity bill of Rs6 to Rs6.50 per unit?” He said a gas cargo that previously cost around $30 million was now costing more than $95 million, making it necessary to take measures to reduce fuel costs. “We carried out load-shedding during peak hours to save fuel costs,” the minister said. He clarified that the government had not signed any new agreement with any independent power producer (IPP), adding that incorrect reports had appeared in the media on the matter. During the meeting, PML-N MNA Rana Muhammad Hayat said there was a lot of discussion but electricity prices had not come down. “There is so much load-shedding that it has become difficult for us to go among the people,” he said. Hayat also criticised the performance of the Discos, but ended up blaming the policymakers and the ministry for the state of affairs in the power sector. “What can the Discos do, minister sahab ? You switch off the electricity,” he said. The PML-N lawmaker said the government’s policies gave the impression that it was working primarily to meet the requirements of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), rather than addressing people’s problems. “Yes, I feel like we are working not for the country but only for the IMF,” he said. The minister, however, responded that Hayat was making an irresponsible statement at a responsible forum.

Indian delegates attempt to interrupt Ayaz Sadiq’s address at Commonwealth conference. ISLAMABAD: Indian delegates reportedly attempted to interrupt National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq’s address at the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa, as he spoke about climate adaptation and climate justice. According to information available, the Indian delegates repeatedly sought to intervene during Sadiq’s speech, with footage showing attempts to get hold of the microphone and disrupt the proceedings. Sadiq had raised the issue of “water terrorism” during his address without naming any country, in the context of broader concerns over climate change, water resources and climate justice. The Indian delegates’ attempts to seize the microphone affected the atmosphere of the session, prompting direct intervention by the host and the Jamaican speaker, who asked them either to remain silent or leave the hall. Meanwhile, other participants advised the Indian delegates to listen patiently to Speaker Sadiq’s address. Despite the disruption, the discussion on climate adaptation and climate justice continued. In his address, Speaker Sadiq, without naming any country or delegation, presented a principled position on tackling climate change and stressed the responsibilities of the international community. He raised issues, including the sudden surge of water in rivers and the withholding of water, without naming any country. Speaker Sadiq said climate adaptation policies should be formulated with effective public participation, adding that oversight by democratic institutions was indispensable to policies aimed at addressing climate change. He added that climate change was affecting various spheres of life, including food, water and health, noting that Pakistan was among the countries most affected by climate change. “Tackling climate change requires climate justice and the inclusion of democratic institutions,” he said, adding that parliamentary dialogue on global challenges such as climate change should be serious, purposeful and constructive. He said the role of parliaments was important in the practical implementation of climate policies and that international climate finance should come under parliamentary oversight. “The Parliament of Pakistan is playing an important role in climate adaptation through legislation, budgetary oversight and committees,” he said, adding that the inclusion of women, youth and other segments of society was indispensable to addressing climate change. “To deal with climate risks, parliaments should benefit from mutual experiences,” he said, adding that to meet the challenges of climate change, parliaments should promote cooperation and meaningful dialogue rather than differences. “Strong democratic institutions are indispensable for strong and vibrant societies,” Speaker Sadiq said, adding that climate adaptation could be effective only with fair financial assistance and democratic accountability. The Indus Water Treaty (IWT) remains a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year — a move that was followed by a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025. Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. In August, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in the Hague also ordered India to uphold the IWT with Pakistan and suspend work on a hydro project in occupied Kashmir.

Yemeni forces clash with Houthis near Saudi border. Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters near the Saudi border, with AFP footage showing soldiers in armoured vehicles and trucks pushing across desert terrain under the crackle of machine-gun fire. The Houthis also released footage on Wednesday of the fighting in the Al-Jawf area, as well as a video purporting to show the downing of a fighter jet belonging to Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s main backer. “The First Division Emergency Forces are advancing on the Al-Labanat front and, God willing, will reach Houthi positions,” Waleed Al-Mahajeri, operations commander of the government’s Fifth Brigade, told an embedded AFP journalist on Tuesday. He went on to claim that the “Houthi militias are retreating and fleeing across all fronts”. AFP footage showed the soldiers firing heavy machine guns, artillery and RPGs at distant targets, as well as the bodies of Houthi fighters and entrenchments the government forces said the group had abandoned as they fell back. “Al-Masariya Hill has been liberated, as has Al-Labanat camp, and the advance is continuing towards Al-Tebab al-Soud,” said soldier Abu Mithaq. This handout picture released on September 16, 2026 by Ansarullah Media Centre shows what the Houthi authorities said is the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that was shot down in the central province of Marib. — AFP Yemen’s civil war roared back to life in July after lying mostly dormant since 2022, with the Houthis making rapid advances that saw them seize the entirety of the country’s Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea’s southern tip. The group has long held large parts of the country’s north, including the capital Sanaa. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have scrambled to respond to the new offensive, and Saudi airstrikes have failed to roll back the Houthis’ gains. In their own video, Houthi fighters can be seen racing across the desert in pick-up trucks, at one point firing on an advancing vehicle. “We are conducting now, God willing, an operation to… cut off the enemy,” one of the fighters can be heard saying. A separate video issued by the group includes night-vision footage appearing to show a projectile striking a fighter jet. Other scenes show the wreckage of a downed plane, with a charred tailfin bearing the Saudi flag. The Houthis said on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet using a locally made missile. Earlier today, the Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthi rebels of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. The Houthis swiftly rejected as a “lie” Riyadh’s report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year. “The claims about targeting Makkah are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis’ politburo wrote on X.

Petroleum dealers demand govt devise mechanism for fuel subsidy reimbursement. KARACHI: Petroleum dealers have called on the government to devise a mechanism for reimbursing the fuel subsidy, which is set to take effect across the country from midnight on Wednesday. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Under the scheme, a relief of Rs100 per litre on a monthly quota of 20 litres will be provided to bike and auto owners, while those owning small vehicles of up to 800cc will get a relief of Rs100 per litre for a monthly quota of 30 litres. “We welcome the government’s move for the benefit of the public, but our businesses should not suffer,” Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) Chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh said. He was addressing an emergency press conference on Wednesday along with other office-bearers of the association. “The fuel subsidy scheme started in Islamabad at midnight on Tuesday and will be launched across the country from tonight,” Malik said. He added: “But our issue is that petroleum dealers are asking us: who will pay the subsidy amount and when?” He explained that no fuel station could afford to bear a loss of Rs100 per litre or wait for delayed payments for a long period. “We have approached the Petroleum Division, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and even the Finance Ministry to get an answer to one simple question,” Khuda Bakhsh said. He added that the confusion was compounded by the fact that it appeared none of the authorities themselves were aware of the issue. “The officials of Ogra and oil marketing companies say that the Petroleum Division will possibly pay the subsidy amount, whereas Petroleum Division officials maintain that the payments will be made by the Finance Ministry. A Finance Ministry official has assured us that the State Bank will release the funds within a day or two,” he added. He also maintained that the federal government had assured the dealers that they would be taken into confidence before the launch of the fuel relief package. “The government has to understand that if payments are not reimbursed on time, many dealers will stop participating in the scheme, as many previous promises made by the government were not fulfilled,” he added. PPDA Vice Chairman Tariq Hassan said that around 14,000 dealers across the country had been trying to contact the government for the past three days, but whenever the government wanted to enforce something, it stopped communication. Another vice chairman, Anwar Kamal, said that if the scheme was to be successful, the government must negotiate with dealers. He also rejected the government’s proposed “smart lockdown”. He added that billions of rupees belonging to dealers should not remain tied up for a long period under the scheme. Meanwhile, Minister Shaza Fatima announced on Wednesday night that the issue related to the forwarding of SMS messages from preloaded packages and low balances had been resolved. “The prime minister has made the SMS for the fuel subsidy available free of charge, and Jazz has completed the system shift. Other telecom companies will also do so by Thursday,” she added.

‘Belligerent action’: Pakistan protests Indian Navy vessel’s 'provocative' manoeuvre near PN vessel. Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the Charge d’Affaires of the Indian High Commission and lodged a “strong protest” over a “highly provocative and unacceptable” action by an Indian Navy vessel in Pakistan’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on Sept 15, the Foreign Office (FO) said. According to the FO, the incident occurred while the Pakistan Navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26 . The FO said that the Indian vessel carried out “aggressive manoeuvres” in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels. The ministry termed the incident a “serious violation of international law” as well as the 1991 bilateral agreement on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troop Movements. It said the incident also risked escalating tensions in the region. The Indian diplomat was asked to convey to New Delhi that Pakistan “strongly rejects” the “belligerent Indian action” and urged India to strictly adhere to international law and bilateral agreements, particularly those intended to prevent incidents at sea. The FO added that Pakistan’s Charge d’Affaires in New Delhi would lodge a similar demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs. Pakistan also called on the international community to urge India to refrain from what it described as “irresponsible actions” that could further destabilise South Asia. “The region can ill-afford to remain perpetually hostage to India’s reckless pursuit of conflict and instability,” the ministry said. India’s Ministry of External Affairs also summoned Pakistan’s envoy in New Delhi earlier today and issued a demarche over the incident. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation . After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed six Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight . After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire . In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

US Fed delivers first rate hike since 2023. WASHINGTON: The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised interest rates in the world’s largest economy by 25 basis points to tackle stubbornly high inflation, a move sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has demanded lower rates. The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent, citing “elevated” inflation and adding that the rate hike would support a “timelier return” to its 2pc target for the metric. Addressing a press conference after the rate decision, US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh stre­ssed that the central bank’s decision to raise interest rates, the first since 2023, was not influenced by financial markets. “We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation,” Warsh told the press conference. “I’ll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision.” He said that the central bank’s independence comes from staying focused on its objectives, in comments that come amid political pressure for lower interest rates. “Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane,” Warsh said. “We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That’s how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them. “Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” he told a press conference. A majority of Fed policymakers expect at least one more rate hike to be necessary before the end of the year, according to the central bank’s Summary of Economic Projections, also published Wednesday. Published in Dawn, September 17th, 2026
